articles.headline: BTS in Lima: big concerts, a famous hat and lots of visitors
articles.standfirst: The South Korean band played three concerts in Lima, and its leader visited a very old pyramid.
body: BTS, the famous band from South Korea, came to Peru this month. The group played three concerts at San Marcos Stadium in Lima. The first concert was on Wednesday 7 October, and the other two were on 9 and 10 October. Thousands of fans, who call themselves ARMY, went to see them.

The day after the first concert, the band's leader, RM, visited Huaca Pucllana. It is a very old pyramid in the Miraflores district of Lima. People from the Lima culture built it with adobe and clay between about 200 and 700 AD. RM shared photos of his visit on Instagram. In one photo, he is wearing a colourful chullo, a traditional Peruvian wool hat.

The concerts are good for Peru's economy too. The Ministry of Foreign Trade and Tourism says visitors will spend about US$18.7 million on hotels, food, transport and other things. The minister said that big international events bring more tourists to the country.

people who like a singer, band or team very much

soft earth that becomes hard when it is dry or hot
done or made in the same way for a very long time

articles.exam: A2 Key · Reading Part 2 (true / false / doesn't say)
articles.headline: A new record on Mars: Perseverance drives farther than any other rover
articles.standfirst: NASA's robot car has now travelled about 45 kilometres on the red planet.
body: Perseverance is a robot car, or rover, from NASA. It landed on Mars in February 2021, in a place called Jezero Crater. Since then, it has driven slowly in and around the crater and studied the rocks there.

Last Sunday, Perseverance broke a record. Its total distance went past 28.06 miles, or about 45 kilometres. Except on Earth, no vehicle in the solar system has driven farther. The old record belonged to Opportunity, a smaller NASA rover. Opportunity drove on Mars from 2004 until 2018, when it stopped working.

The team thought Perseverance would break the record in August. But then the rover found some interesting light-coloured rocks. They may be some of the oldest rocks ever studied on Mars, so Perseverance stayed near them for two months. For the scientists, the rocks are more important than the record. The rover will probably drive many more kilometres in the next few years.

a big round hole in the ground

articles.headline: A singer, a small shop and a mechanical bird called Molly
articles.standfirst: One angry post from a famous singer brought crowds – and problems – to a toy shop in New York.
body: Art of Play is a small shop that sells toys, games and puzzles in Cobble Hill, a quiet part of Brooklyn in New York. On one wall of the shop there is a wooden mechanical bird called Molly, which can sing and dance.

Last Saturday, the American singer Kelly Clarkson visited the shop for about five minutes. She liked the bird and wanted to buy it. Later, she complained on social media. She said that the staff had looked at her as if she couldn't afford the bird, which she said cost $15,000. She compared her experience to a famous scene in the 1990 film Pretty Woman, where shop assistants are rude to a customer.

The shop told a different story. It said that Molly is fixed to the wall and is not for sale. According to the shop, an employee told the singer that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000. The shop also offered her a different singing bird, made by a clock-making company in Germany, for $2,000.

After the singer's posts, thousands of people attacked the small business online, and the owner said that he and his staff had received threats. "It's been a surreal experience," the shop said. On Wednesday, when BBC reporters visited, there were more journalists than customers inside. Molly was still on the wall – but now with a joke price tag of $15 million.

articles.headline: Europe's 'roof' is getting a little lower
articles.standfirst: Surveyors say Mont Blanc lost more than a metre of height in a year.
body: Mont Blanc in France is the highest mountain in western Europe, and people often call it 'the roof of Europe'. But its height is not the same every year. Last month, a team of surveyors climbed to the top to measure it again. On Wednesday they announced the result: the summit is now 4,807.47 metres above sea level. That is 1.29 metres lower than in 2025.

How can a mountain change its height? The rock of Mont Blanc is about 4,792 metres high, and on top of the rock there is a thick cap of snow and ice. Heat, wind, snow and rain make this cap thicker or thinner, so the summit goes up and down. The highest result was in 2007, when it reached 4,810.90 metres. The lowest in recent years was in 2023.
The surveyors have checked the mountain regularly since 2001. They use very exact satellite technology, and drones help them to make a detailed model of the snow and ice.

The experts say that one year's change does not tell us everything about climate change. However, lower down in the Alps the ice is melting fast. This summer was the hottest on record in western Europe, and Swiss scientists say Switzerland has lost one-fifth of its ice in the last five years. The leader of the expedition said that, on one glacier, climbers now cross a stream where there used to be ice.

articles.headline: Built to last: a 5,000-year-old city gets ready for El Niño
articles.standfirst: Archaeologists at Caral are protecting the ancient Sacred City from heavy rain – and learning from the people who built it.
body: The Sacred City of Caral, in the Supe Valley north of Lima, was built by one of the oldest civilisations in the world, which developed there between 3000 and 1800 BC. Now, as Peru prepares for the heavy rain that El Niño is expected to bring, the archaeologists who look after the site are working hard to protect its ancient buildings.

According to Aldemar Crispín, the Ministry of Culture's chief archaeologist at Caral, the work is "quite intensive". His team has installed drainage channels and water outlets, and roofs and coverings are being put over the structures so that rain does not fall directly on them. Windbreaks have also been set up to stop the wind from wearing away the walls. The work is being paid for with both public and private money.

Interestingly, some of the monuments were already prepared for bad weather because of the way they were built. Their builders used a technique called shicras: they filled bags made of plant fibres with stones of different sizes and used them to build walls that could resist earthquakes, which are common on Peru's central coast. A similar method has been used in recent times in Japan. The people of Caral also chose to build their settlements away from riverbanks. In 2017, a coastal El Niño destroyed many crops in the Supe Valley, but it did not destroy the archaeological sites.

Research at Caral began 32 years ago, and discoveries are still being made. Recently, archaeologists found two small clay figures, one male and one female, near the Main Residential Complex. They may help to explain how these people saw nature and themselves. To celebrate the anniversary, the site will hold a festival called Caral Raymi on 23 and 24 October, with a ceremony for Pachamama, coloured lights at night, and traditional music and dance.

articles.headline: An elephant's sad journey wins the world's top wildlife photo prize
articles.standfirst: From glowing mushrooms to a curious octopus, this year's Wildlife Photographer of the Year winners show nature at its most surprising.
body: A. The overall winner of Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 is Federico Veronesi from Italy. While he was tracking elephants in Namibia, he noticed unusual drag marks in a dry riverbed. Then a female elephant appeared, carrying her dead calf between her tusk and her trunk. Scientists know that both Asian and African elephants react to death in complex ways: they make sounds, guard the body and even handle the bones. Veronesi's photograph, The Aftermath, captures one of these rare moments.

B. In the Natural Artistry category, Michał Michalski from Poland used a slow shutter speed to create something close to a painting. When a sparrowhawk frightened a mixed flock of goldfinches and bramblings out of a sunflower field, the moving birds became a blur, making bare birch trees look as if they still had their autumn leaves.

C. Agorastos Papatsanis from Greece won the Plants and Fungi category on the lower slopes of Mount Olympus. By shining ultraviolet light on mushrooms growing from a rotting log, he made their stems glow bright yellow. He experimented for some time before finding the strongest effect.

D. Under the sea off Cornwall, in the UK, Aaron Sanders was diving when he spotted the marks of an octopus's suckers through a thin piece of kelp. Slowly, a single eye appeared. Diver and octopus stayed perfectly still, watching each other with what seemed like shared curiosity. His picture, A Watchful Eye, won the Animal Portraits prize.

E. Not every winning image is simply beautiful. Alex Visbal from Colombia photographed a lake in Utah, in the US, which is divided by a man-made line. On one side, the water is pink because of microbes that thrive in extremely salty water. The lake's ecology is in decline because of industry, water being taken upstream and climate change, although the area has since been placed under conservation management. All the winning photographs will be shown at the Natural History Museum in London from 16 October 2026 until July 2027.

articles.headline: Rising from the ashes: the 'impossible' planet around a dead star
articles.standfirst: Astronomers think they have found a rare second-generation world – and the first clue had been hiding in data collected in 1999.
body: When a star like our Sun runs out of nuclear fuel, it throws off its outer layers and collapses into a white dwarf: a small, extremely dense remnant that cools very slowly. Planets can sometimes survive this violent transformation. What astronomers had not expected to find was a planet that appears to have been born afterwards, out of the dying star's own debris.

Yet that is precisely what a team led by researchers at the University of Warwick, in the UK, believe they have found around a white dwarf known as HS 0209+0832. Their findings, published this month in the journal Nature Astronomy, began not with a new observation but with an old one. Measurements made by NASA's Hubble Space Telescope in 1999 contained about 100 chemical features that nobody had managed to identify for more than two decades. Using an updated database of chemical signatures, doctoral researcher Jamie Williams discovered that many of them matched niobium, a heavy element never before detected in the atmosphere of a white dwarf.

That detail matters because elements such as niobium are produced only by dying stars, which then eject them. The team suspects that some of this ejected material gathered into a disc and eventually formed a gas giant roughly the size of Jupiter. Further support came from NASA's TESS satellite, which monitored the white dwarf for four months and recorded a regular change in its brightness every 4.4 days. That would be consistent with a planet orbiting only about 3.7 million miles (roughly six million kilometres) from the star, far closer than Mercury is to the Sun.

At such close range, intense radiation is probably stripping away the planet's atmosphere. The escaping gas may form a comet-like tail, settle into a disc and finally fall onto the star – a process which would explain the unusual heavy elements Hubble detected. Even so, Williams believes the planet is likely to survive, since the radiation should weaken as the white dwarf cools. He compared the discovery to finding a planet that has "risen from the ashes" of the star it once orbited.

If it is confirmed, this will be the first convincing example of a second-generation planet orbiting a white dwarf. The next step is to search for other white dwarfs with similar chemical fingerprints, to establish whether such worlds are genuinely rare or simply hard to find.

articles.headline: Two days off for everyone? Brazil votes to shorten the working week
articles.standfirst: A change to the constitution will cut the standard week from 44 to 40 hours. Supporters predict better-rested workers; critics warn of higher prices.
body: Brazil's Congress has approved one of the biggest changes to workers' rights since the country returned to democracy in 1988. A constitutional amendment will reduce the standard working week from 44 hours to 40 and guarantee employees two days off a week, without any reduction in their salary. More than 30 million workers are expected to benefit. Celebrating the result on social media, Lula said the change would give people more time to rest, to be with their families and to look after themselves.

The measure had already passed the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house, in May. On Wednesday, the Senate backed it by an overwhelming 75 votes to one. The vote came less than two weeks before the second round of Brazil's presidential election on 25 October, and both candidates ended up supporting it: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who had championed the change, and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who had previously opposed it but said he had changed his mind because of its popularity. Opinion polls suggest the idea is very popular; one national survey found that almost 70% of Brazilians were in favour.

The change will not happen overnight. After a two-month grace period, the week will first be cut to 42 hours and later to 40, so it will take more than a year to come fully into effect. For some workers, the impact could be considerable. Luciana de Almeida, a 36-year-old supermarket cashier in Rio de Janeiro who currently works six days a week, told the BBC that it would "make a lot of difference" to her life.

Not everyone is convinced, however. Critics argue that shorter hours will push up production costs, which businesses will eventually pass on to consumers in the form of higher prices. Supporters counter that people who enjoy two full days of rest will be fresher, and therefore more productive, during the hours they do work.

The debate echoes discussions in many countries about how much of our lives should be spent at work. Whether Brazil's reform produces a healthier, more efficient workforce or simply a more expensive economy is a question that economists far beyond Brazil are likely to follow closely.
